title: 1 Chronicles 1:1–16
context: Chronicles opens not with a battle or a king, but with names: from Adam to Noah’s three sons, then the families of Japheth and Ham. The first sixteen verses are a compressed form of the early genealogies in Genesis 5 and of the Japheth and Ham sections of Genesis 10. The Chronicler gives the names without the ages, deaths, or longer geographical notices of those chapters. The point of the opening, shared by both traditions, is to place Israel among the world’s families, not as a people without a human beginning. A few spellings differ from the Genesis lists and should be named as differences, not forced into a single explanation: 1:6 has Diphath where Genesis 10:3 has Riphath, and 1:7 has Rodanim where Genesis 10:4 has Dodanim. The lists are not to be allegorized, and uncertain identifications of ancient sites or peoples should be left open.

verses.arminianNotes:
The book begins, “Adam, Seth, Enosh,” with no verb and no ages. The same three names open the line after Adam in Genesis 5, where the story is told with years and deaths. Here only the names are given, and the list runs on into the next verses.

Arminian readers take this as a real human beginning. Israel’s story is set inside the first families of the earth, not outside them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear a deliberate start at Adam, the same starting point as Genesis 5, now stated as a bare succession of names.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.arminianNotes:
The line continues: Kenan, Mahalalel, and Jared. These are the next names in Genesis 5, again without the years recorded there. WEB uses Kenan in both books, not a different spelling.

Arminian readers receive the names as a historical succession carried forward, a line of real fathers and sons, not as a code to be decoded.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to allegorize the list. The Chronicler is moving the reader down the same pre-flood line already told in Genesis 5, now in compressed form.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.arminianNotes:
“Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech” follow, still in the order of Genesis 5. That chapter tells of Enoch’s walk with God and of long lives; this verse does not retell those scenes. It only keeps the names in place.

Arminian readers let the silence stand. The Chronicler assumes the earlier record and does not enlarge or spiritualize these three names here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise treat the verse as a faithful, shortened form of the Genesis 5 succession, not as a new story about Enoch or Lamech.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.arminianNotes:
The pre-flood line closes: “Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.” Genesis 5:32 names the same three sons of Noah. The world’s families that follow will be grouped under these three, as in Genesis 10.

Arminian readers hear a real family at the hinge of the flood. From these four names the Chronicler will turn outward to the nations.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the same hinge. Noah and his three sons stand where Genesis placed them, so that Israel’s later line can be shown among the families of the earth.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.text: The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.” The seven names match Genesis 10:2. The Chronicler starts with Japheth, as Genesis 10 does, before Ham and Shem.

Arminian readers take the list as a record of real peoples descended from Japheth, named with the same care as Israel will be named later.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a straightforward parallel to Genesis 10:2. The nations are catalogued, not ranked into a hidden typology.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.text: The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Diphath, and Togarmah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Diphath, and Togarmah.” Genesis 10:3 has Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The difference is the middle name: Diphath here, Riphath there. The two spellings should be named as they stand and not forced into one explanation.

Arminian readers can note the parallel and the variant without deciding a scribal history the text does not tell.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise leave Diphath and Riphath as a difference between the lists. The verse still places Gomer’s sons among the world’s families.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.text: The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Rodanim.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Rodanim.” Genesis 10:4 has the first three names and then Dodanim, not Rodanim. The variant should be reported neutrally, as a difference, without a forced solution.

Arminian readers keep both readings in view as the two lists give them, and they do not allegorize Javan’s sons as types of later churches or empires.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to harmonize Rodanim and Dodanim into a single required spelling. The parallel is Genesis 10:4; the names differ, and the list still serves the Chronicler’s opening purpose.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.text: The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.” The four names match Genesis 10:6. From them will come African, Egyptian, and Canaanite families, still as kin in the table of nations.

Arminian readers hear a real kinship that later conflict will not erase. Ham’s sons are named in the same world-family as Japheth’s and, soon, Shem’s.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same four names as Genesis 10:6, a sober placing of Egypt and Canaan among the peoples God has made.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.text: The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raama, Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.
verses.arminianNotes:
Cush’s sons are Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raama, and Sabteca, and Raamah’s sons are Sheba and Dedan. Genesis 10:7 has Sabtah and Raamah, spellings that differ slightly from Sabta and Raama here, while this same verse then uses Raamah. The variation should be named, not explained away.

Arminian readers treat the list as a genuine family record with small differences from its Genesis parallel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the parallel in Genesis 10:7 and the uneven spellings, without building a doctrine or a harmonizing theory on them.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.text: Cush became the father of Nimrod. He began to be a mighty one on the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Cush became the father of Nimrod. He began to be a mighty one on the earth.” The wording matches the opening of Genesis 10:8. Chronicles does not go on to the hunter saying, the kingdom in Shinar, or the Assyrian cities of Genesis 10:9–12.

Arminian readers take the shorter form as a choice to name Nimrod without retelling that whole scene. The verse is not an allegory of later tyranny.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the parallel and the omission in view. Genesis 10 says more about Nimrod; this verse records his might and his place under Cush, and then moves on.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.text: Mizraim became the father of Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim,
verses.arminianNotes:
Mizraim’s line begins: “Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim,” and the list continues in the next verse. The same four names, in the same order, stand in Genesis 10:13.

Arminian readers receive these peoples as historical families from Egypt’s ancestor, listed rather than described, and not as symbols to be decoded.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear a compressed parallel to Genesis 10:13. The Chronicler is still mapping the sons of Ham among the world’s families.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.text: Pathrusim, Casluhim (where the Philistines came from), and Caphtorim.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Mizraim list ends with Pathrusim, Casluhim, “where the Philistines came from” and Caphtorim. Genesis 10:14 has the same three names and a similar notice, “which the Philistines descended from” The wording differs slightly; the fact named is the same kinship.

Arminian readers remember that later enemies are still recorded here as relatives in the human family.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name the parallel and the small difference of phrasing, without forcing one English wording on the other list.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.text: Canaan became the father of Sidon his firstborn, Heth,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Canaan became the father of Sidon his firstborn, Heth,” Genesis 10:15 names the same firstborn and Heth. The Canaanite list that follows will run through verse 16, as Genesis 10:15–18 does, with some difference of singular and plural forms.

Arminian readers take Sidon and Heth as real ancestors of peoples in the land, not as moral types.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers read a close parallel to Genesis 10:15. The Chronicler is still locating Canaan inside the world’s families before Israel’s later story in that land.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.text: the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgashite,
verses.arminianNotes:
The list continues with “the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgashite,”. Genesis 10:16 has the same three as plurals: the Jebusites, the Amorites, and the Girgashites. The peoples named are the same; the English number differs.

Arminian readers note that difference without making a doctrine of it, and they do not turn the names into allegories of later sins.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise report the parallel and the singular-and-plural difference as a fact of the two lists, not as a problem that must be solved here.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.text: the Hivite, the Arkite, the Sinite,
verses.arminianNotes:
Next are “the Hivite, the Arkite, the Sinite,” matching the three peoples of Genesis 10:17, again in the singular here and the plural there.

Arminian readers keep the names as a record of Canaan’s families. Identifications of exact later towns should remain modest where the verse itself does not locate them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to press uncertain site identifications. The Chronicler is following the Genesis 10 list, in shorter form, still among the world’s families.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.

verses.text: the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Hamite section closes: “the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite.” Genesis 10:18 has the same three in the plural and then describes the spread and borders of the Canaanites, which this verse does not repeat.

Arminian readers take the three names as the end of this opening Canaan list, a historical close rather than a coded map.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the parallel and the omission of Genesis 10’s border notice. The unit ends with Ham’s line catalogued, and Shem will follow.

Both traditions read the Chronicler’s work here as a real placing of Israel among the world’s families, not as a puzzle of hidden symbols.
